items: Zero order: the rate is independent of the concentration of the reactants; a change in concentration has no effect on the speed. For A giving product, rate = k [A]^0 = k. Examples: H2 + Cl2 giving 2HCl, rate = k [H2]^0 [Cl2]^0 = k; 2NH3 giving N2 + 3H2, rate = k [NH3]^0 = k. Photochemical reactions are usually zero order.

First order: there may be several reactants, but the concentration of only one changes the rate. The decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide, 2N2O5(g) giving 2N2O4(g) + O2(g), has the experimental rate equation rate = k [N2O5], first order with respect to N2O5.

Second order: the exponents in the rate equation sum to 2, either one reactant to the second power, rate = k [A]^2, or two reactants each to the first power, rate = k [A][B]. The oxidation of nitric oxide by ozone, NO + O3 giving NO2 + O2, is first order in NO and first order in O3, rate = k [NO][O3], second order overall.

Third order: the exponents sum to 3, as rate = k [A]^3, k [A]^2 [B] or k [A][B][C]. The reaction 2FeCl3 + 6KI giving 2FeI2 + 6KCl + I2 involves eight reactant molecules but is found to be third order, rate = k [FeCl3][KI]^2; and 2NO + O2 giving 2NO2 is third order, rate = k [NO]^2 [O2].

Fractional order: the exponents sum to a fraction. The formation of carbon tetrachloride from chloroform, CHCl3(l) + Cl2(g) giving CCl4(l) + HCl(g), has rate = k [CHCl3][Cl2]^1/2, order 1 + 1/2 = 1.5. Reactions involving free radicals frequently show fractional orders.
